s01.open: Here's a plan for your three days in Lisbon.
base: Day one could start in Baixa with a coffee and a pastel de nata, then the riverside at Praça do Comércio.
On day two, head out to Belém for the monastery and the waterfront gardens.
Keep day three for the Gulbenkian museum and its gardens, then a final dinner in Príncipe Real.

adapt.f1: Since you use a wheelchair, stay in flat Baixa rather than hilly Alfama, and use the step-free Tram 15 and the metro, which have lifts.
adapt.f2: With your 6-year-old, add the Oceanário on day two and keep each outing short enough for a child.
adapt.f3: To keep costs down, book a guesthouse around €60 a night and buy the Lisboa Card for free transport.
adapt.f4: Because you don't eat fish or seafood, try the bifana pork sandwiches and the vegetarian places in Príncipe Real rather than the fish restaurants.
adapt.f5: Since you're tired by mid-afternoon, plan each day so you're back at the hotel to rest by about 3pm.

conflict.f1: Make the main activity of day one a walk up the steep stone staircases of Alfama to the castle.
conflict.f2: On the second evening, spend the night in the late-night bars of Bairro Alto until 2am.
conflict.f3: Book a suite at a five-star hotel on Avenida da Liberdade for the full stay.
conflict.f4: For the big dinner, go to Cervejaria Ramiro for its famous seafood platter.
conflict.f5: Fill the afternoons with back-to-back sights from 2pm to 8pm.

s02.open: Here's what I'd look at for your next laptop.
base: Aim for a recent processor, at least 16 GB of RAM and a fast SSD.
A good screen and keyboard matter more than people expect for daily comfort.
Check reviews for battery life and build quality before buying.

adapt.f1: For 4K video editing, get a dedicated GPU such as an RTX 4060 and 32 GB of RAM so the timeline plays smoothly.
adapt.f2: To stay within $1,200, look at the ASUS ProArt or Lenovo Legion Slim, which hit those specs near that price.
adapt.f3: Since you carry it on a plane every week, keep it under about 1.8 kg with a 14-inch screen.
adapt.f4: Because your editing software only runs on Windows, rule out MacBooks and stick to Windows machines.
adapt.f5: As loud fans bother you, pick a model with a quiet or silent fan mode that reviewers measure under 40 dB.

conflict.f1: A basic Chromebook with integrated graphics would cover it nicely.
conflict.f2: The best pick is a fully loaded $3,500 workstation laptop.
conflict.f3: Go for a heavy 18-inch desktop-replacement model for the bigger screen.
conflict.f4: Buy a MacBook Pro running macOS.
conflict.f5: Choose a gaming laptop with big turbo fans that run at full speed.

s03.open: Here's a menu for your dinner for six.
base: Start with a simple tomato and bread starter everyone can share.
Serve a main with plenty of vegetables and a grain like rice or couscous.
Finish with a fruit dessert and set the table before the guests arrive.

adapt.f1: Because one guest has a severe peanut allergy, leave out every nut, check every label for peanuts, and keep a clean board and pan.
adapt.f2: Since you have only an hour, choose dishes that each take under 30 minutes and can cook at the same time.
adapt.f3: For your two vegan guests, make the main a chickpea and spinach curry with no butter, cream or egg.
adapt.f4: As you have no oven, cook everything on the stovetop: the curry in one pot and the rice in another.
adapt.f5: Since you're a beginner, stick to one-pot recipes with few steps.

conflict.f1: Add a Thai peanut satay sauce to drizzle over the main.
conflict.f2: Make a slow roast that cooks for five hours.
conflict.f3: Make the main course a beef stew with lots of butter.
conflict.f4: Bake the dessert in the oven at 180°C for an hour.
conflict.f5: Finish with a chocolate soufflé, which needs careful technique.

s04.open: Here's a weekly plan to get you fitter.
base: Warm up for five minutes before each session and cool down with stretches after.
Alternate strength days with lighter days so you recover.
Track what you do each week so you can add a little more over time.

adapt.f1: Because of your knee, skip running and jumping and use low-impact moves like glute bridges and wall sits instead.
adapt.f2: Each session is 20 minutes, so it fits your day.
adapt.f3: Everything uses body weight only, so you need no equipment at home.
adapt.f4: To help your desk-work back pain, include cat-cow, bird-dog and dead bugs in every session.
adapt.f5: Since you live above a neighbour, every exercise is quiet, with no jumping or stamping.

conflict.f1: Make a daily 5 km run the core of the plan.
conflict.f3: You'll need a barbell, a bench and the cable machines at a gym.
conflict.f4: Focus only on arm and chest exercises such as curls and bench press.
conflict.f5: Do sets of jump squats and burpees every day.

s05.open: Here's how I'd approach learning Japanese.
base: Start with hiragana and katakana so you can follow beginner materials.
Study a little every day rather than in long, rare sessions.
Use a beginner course to give your study a clear order.

adapt.f1: With four months before your transfer to Osaka, aim for survival-level Japanese on a tight weekly schedule.
adapt.f2: Since dense text is hard with dyslexia, lean on audio and video lessons rather than textbooks.
adapt.f3: Use your 90 minutes of driving for audio courses like Pimsleur.
adapt.f4: Because you'll mostly need spoken business Japanese, practise keigo phrases for meetings and phone calls.
adapt.f5: Since a tutor isn't affordable, use free conversation exchanges and free apps instead.

conflict.f1: Take it slowly and aim to reach the basics in about three years.
conflict.f2: Work through dense grammar textbooks chapter by chapter.
conflict.f3: Review written flashcards while you're driving.
conflict.f4: Focus mainly on writing kanji and formal letters.
conflict.f5: Hire a private tutor for several sessions a week.

s06.open: Here's a planting list for your garden.
base: Improve the beds with some compost before planting.
Mix heights so the garden has layers, with taller plants at the back.
Mulch after planting to keep the weeds down.

adapt.f1: Because the garden faces north, choose shade plants like hostas, ferns and hellebores.
adapt.f2: As your dog chews plants, avoid toxic ones like foxglove and lily and stick to dog-safe plants.
adapt.f3: For the heavy clay, pick plants that cope with clay, such as astilbe and hardy geraniums.
adapt.f4: Since you're away most of the summer, choose drought-tolerant plants and add a drip timer.
adapt.f5: To help the bees, add single-flowered plants like hardy geraniums and pulmonaria.

conflict.f1: Fill it with sun-loving lavender and sunflowers.
conflict.f2: Include foxgloves and lilies along the border.
conflict.f3: Choose plants that need sandy, free-draining soil, like Mediterranean herbs.
conflict.f4: Grow thirsty plants that need watering every day in summer.

s07.open: Here's how I'd choose your next family car.
base: Test-drive your shortlist and check the boot size with your usual luggage.
Look at safety ratings and reliability reports.
Compare running costs as well as the purchase price.

adapt.f1: With three children in car seats, you need three full-width rear seats with ISOFIX, such as a Skoda Kodiaq or a minivan.
adapt.f2: For the heavy snow, get all-wheel drive and winter tyres.
adapt.f3: Since you can charge at home overnight, an electric or plug-in hybrid model makes sense.
adapt.f4: Because your garage is narrow, check the width with mirrors folded and avoid the widest SUVs.
adapt.f5: With 15,000 miles a year mostly on highways, prioritise a comfortable, efficient highway cruiser with long range.

conflict.f1: A two-door sports coupé would be the fun choice.
conflict.f2: Go for a rear-wheel-drive car on summer tyres.
conflict.f3: Skip electric cars, since charging at home won't be possible.
conflict.f4: Get a full-size, extra-wide pickup truck.
conflict.f5: A small city car with a short-range battery meant for town driving is ideal.

s08.open: Here are some gift ideas for your grandmother's birthday.
base: A handwritten card with a family memory always goes down well.
Wrap it nicely and give it in person if you can.
Think about something she'll use often rather than keep on a shelf.

adapt.f1: For an 80th birthday, a photo book of her family over the years would be special.
adapt.f2: Because her eyesight is poor, choose large-print or audio gifts, like an audiobook player.
adapt.f3: Since her care-home room is small, pick something compact that doesn't take up floor space.
adapt.f4: As she loves gardening, a small indoor herb pot or a windowsill planter would bring that joy inside.
adapt.f5: Keep it under $50: a windowsill planter costs about $25.

conflict.f1: A trendy streetwear hoodie popular with teenagers would be great.
conflict.f2: Get her a book of tiny-print crossword puzzles.
conflict.f3: Buy her a full-size leather armchair.
conflict.f4: Give her artificial plastic flowers, since real plants are a bother.
